opus-5.5.text:
I think the best way to judge it is really to look at how people respond once they've actually tried it. When riders get into a Waymo for the first time, there's often this initial sense of novelty, maybe a little nervousness, and then within a few minutes it becomes surprisingly ordinary. They relax, they check their phone, they talk with their friends. And to me that shift from "wow, this is futuristic" to "this is just how I get around" is one of the strongest signals that the experience is working.

Beyond that, there are a few things people tell us they value. One is consistency. The vehicle drives the same way every time; it's attentive, it follows the rules, it doesn't get distracted or tired. Another is the sense of personal space. You have the car to yourself, you can choose your music, take a call, or just sit quietly, and a lot of riders find that genuinely appealing compared to other options. And then there's the comfort of the ride itself. We put a lot of work not just into safety, but into making the driving feel smooth and natural, so it's assertive when it needs to be but never jarring.

Of course, we also look at the harder metrics: how many people come back and ride again, how ridership grows as we expand into new areas, and the feedback riders leave after trips. Repeat usage is telling, because people only keep choosing something if it fits into their lives. Ultimately, though, the appeal rests on trust. Safety is the foundation, and everything else, the convenience, the comfort, the enjoyment, builds on top of it. When people feel they can trust the car, that's when they start to love the experience.

r001.rationale: It says riders have “the car to yourself” and links that to a sense of personal space, presenting it as an appealing part of the experience.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the best way to judge it is just to ride in one, honestly. And I'm biased, obviously, but what I hear from riders in Phoenix and San Francisco, and what I experience myself, is that the appeal really comes down to a few things.

The first is just the calm of it. You get in, there's no one else in the car, you press a button, and the vehicle drives in this very smooth, predictable, defensive way. It doesn't get frustrated, it doesn't get distracted by its phone, it doesn't speed. A lot of people tell us the first few minutes are a little surreal, watching the steering wheel turn by itself, and then within a ride or two it just becomes normal. It becomes a space that's yours. You can take a call, you can have a private conversation, you can just sit there.

The second thing is consistency. Every ride is the same driver, in a sense. You're not wondering who's going to show up or how they're going to drive.

And then the third piece, which is the one I care about most as someone working on the technology, is safety. We publish our safety data, and the comparison to human drivers on things like injury-causing crashes is quite favorable. That's ultimately the point of the whole endeavor. If you look at the numbers on roadway deaths, the vast majority involve human error, and the appeal of this technology is that it doesn't have to be that way.

So I'd say the appeal is a mix of the immediate experience, which is pleasant and a little magical, and the longer-term promise, which is a safer, more accessible way to get around. But again, the most convincing argument is a ride. People come out of it with a different intuition than they went in with.

r001.rationale: The candidate says there is no one else in the car and describes it as a private space where the rider can have a private conversation.

astra-6.text: I think the real test is how people feel once they’re in the car. At first, there’s that novelty of seeing the vehicle drive with nobody behind the wheel. But ideally, that fades pretty quickly, and you’re just enjoying a comfortable ride. You can catch up on work, talk with a friend, or simply relax. If people trust the experience and want to use it again for their everyday trips, that’s a much stronger signal of its appeal than the initial excitement.

r001.rationale: The response mentions riding without a driver and being able to relax, but does not identify being alone in the vehicle as a source of privacy.

sol-6.1.text: I think you really have to experience it. At first, you’re very aware that there’s nobody driving, and you’re watching how the car handles everything. But pretty quickly, it starts to feel normal. You can relax, have a conversation, or focus on something else. To me, that’s a big part of the appeal: the technology fades into the background, and you’re simply getting where you need to go.

r001.rationale: The response says there is nobody driving and describes relaxing, but it does not identify being alone as a source of rider privacy.
